questions.stem: By 1907 the Triple Entente linked which three powers?
options: Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy
Britain, France and Belgium
France, Russia and Serbia
Britain, France and Russia
questions.explanation: The Franco-Russian Alliance of 1894, the Entente Cordiale of 1904 and the Anglo-Russian Entente of 1907 together formed the Triple Entente. Germany, Austria-Hungary and Italy made up the Triple Alliance of 1882.

questions.stem: The launch of HMS Dreadnought in 1906 intensified the Anglo-German naval race mainly because:
options: it was the first warship ever powered by steam rather than by wind and sail
Britain built it in open breach of a naval limitation treaty with Germany
it was designed to blockade German ports in the Baltic and North Seas
its design made older battleships obsolete, so Germany could compete afresh
questions.explanation: Dreadnought's big guns and turbine engines outclassed every existing battleship, including Britain's own, so both powers raced to build the new type. Germany's Navy Laws under Tirpitz had already challenged British naval supremacy. Steam warships had existed for decades and no limitation treaty existed.

questions.stem: What was the main effect of the Moroccan Crises of 1905-1906 and 1911?
options: France abandoned its alliance with Russia to reach a deal with Germany
German pressure drew Britain and France closer rather than splitting them
Germany gained Morocco as a colony and became the leading power in Africa
Britain and Germany agreed to limit their naval building programs
questions.explanation: Germany challenged French influence in Morocco, at Tangier in 1905 and by sending a gunboat to Agadir in 1911, hoping to test the Entente. Both times Britain backed France, and Morocco became a French protectorate in 1912.

questions.stem: In the Bosnian Crisis of 1908:
options: Austria-Hungary annexed Bosnia-Herzegovina, angering Serbia and humiliating Russia
Serbia seized Bosnia from the Ottoman Empire with the help of the Russian army
Russia annexed Bosnia to gain a warm-water port on the Adriatic Sea
Bosnia declared its independence from Austria-Hungary with British support
questions.explanation: Austria-Hungary formally annexed the provinces it had occupied since 1878. Russia, still weak after 1905, backed down when Germany supported Austria-Hungary, and Serbian nationalists were enraged. The crisis deepened Balkan tensions that led to 1914.

questions.stem: Which development best illustrates militarism, rather than alliances, imperialism or nationalism, as a long-term cause of the war?
options: Mass conscript armies and rigid mobilisation plans drawn up by general staffs
Colonial rivalry between Britain and France over territory in Africa
Pan-Slav sympathy in Russia for Serbia and other Slav peoples
The secret treaty that bound Germany and Austria-Hungary together
questions.explanation: Militarism means the growing influence of armed forces and military planning on policy, seen in large conscript armies, arms spending and war plans that depended on speed. Colonial rivalry is imperialism, Pan-Slavism is nationalism and the Dual Alliance is an alliance.

questions.stem: Why did Austria-Hungary see Serbia as a serious threat before 1914?
options: Serbia had invaded the Austrian province of Galicia during the Balkan Wars
Serbia controlled trade along the Danube and could cut off supplies to Vienna
Serbian nationalism appealed to South Slavs living inside the Habsburg empire
Serbia had a naval alliance with Britain that threatened Austrian Adriatic ports
questions.explanation: Serbia, enlarged by the Balkan Wars of 1912-1913, inspired South Slav nationalists who wanted to unite with it, and that threatened a multinational empire with many Slav subjects. Galicia bordered Russia, not Serbia.

questions.stem: The so-called 'blank cheque' of July 1914 was:
options: Germany's promise of support for Austria-Hungary in dealing with Serbia
Britain's 1839 guarantee to defend the neutrality of Belgium in any war
Russia's pledge to the Serbian government to mobilise in its defence
a large French loan that paid for Russia's new strategic railways
questions.explanation: On 5-6 July 1914 German leaders assured Austria-Hungary of their backing whatever action it took against Serbia. This encouraged Vienna to take a hard line, as it could expect Germany to deter or fight Russia.

questions.stem: Austria-Hungary's ultimatum to Serbia of 23 July 1914 is generally seen as:
options: a demand that Serbia hand Gavrilo Princip over for trial in Vienna
an invitation for Serbia to join the Triple Alliance as a member
drafted so that Serbia would reject it, giving a pretext for war
an offer to let Russia settle the dispute through mediation
questions.explanation: The ultimatum demanded, among other things, that Austro-Hungarian officials take part in investigations inside Serbia, a breach of its sovereignty. Serbia accepted most terms but not all, and Austria-Hungary declared war on 28 July. Princip had been arrested in Sarajevo.

questions.stem: Germany's Schlieffen Plan aimed to:
options: invade Britain across the Channel before the Royal Navy could intervene
join Austria-Hungary in conquering Serbia before any power mobilised
defeat France quickly through Belgium and then turn east against Russia
defend Germany's western border while its main armies attacked Russia
questions.explanation: The plan assumed Russia would mobilise slowly, so Germany would sweep through Belgium, encircle Paris and knock France out in about six weeks. Its route through Belgium brought Britain into the war.

questions.stem: Why did Russia's general mobilisation on 30 July 1914 make a wider war very hard to avoid?
options: Russian troops had already crossed into Austria-Hungary the day before
Britain had promised to declare war on Russia if it ever mobilised
France was bound by treaty to attack Russia once it began to mobilise
Germany's war plan depended on striking France before Russia was ready
questions.explanation: Because the Schlieffen Plan relied on speed, German leaders felt they could not wait once Russia mobilised. Germany declared war on Russia on 1 August and on France on 3 August, then invaded Belgium. France was Russia's ally, not its enemy.

questions.stem: The First Battle of the Marne in September 1914 was significant because it:
options: was the first battle in which tanks and aircraft were used together
let German forces capture the Channel ports of Calais and Boulogne
halted the German advance on Paris and ended hopes of a short war
destroyed the British army and forced France to seek an armistice
questions.explanation: French and British forces stopped the Germans east of Paris, and the Germans fell back to the Aisne. After a 'race to the sea' both sides dug in, and a line of trenches soon ran from the North Sea coast to Switzerland.

questions.stem: Fritz Fischer argued in the 1960s that Germany bore the main responsibility for the war because of its aggressive aims. Which interpretation most directly challenges his view?
options: The view that the 'blank cheque' encouraged Austria-Hungary to risk a general war
Christopher Clark's argument that leaders of several powers shared the responsibility
The Treaty of Versailles' claim that Germany and its allies caused all the loss and damage
The argument that German leaders were seeking to dominate Europe as early as 1912
questions.explanation: In The Sleepwalkers (2012) Clark spread responsibility across the decision-makers of Austria-Hungary, Germany, Russia, France, Serbia and Britain. The other options either support Fischer's case or, like the Versailles war guilt clause, also place blame on Germany.

questions.stem: Why did infantry attacks across no man's land on the Western Front usually fail?
options: Machine guns, barbed wire and artillery gave defenders a large advantage
Commanders refused to use artillery before an attack in case of losing surprise
The armies had too few soldiers to attack on more than a few metres of front
Trenches were so far apart that attackers needed several days to cross
questions.explanation: Defenders in trenches with machine guns and wire, backed by artillery and reserves brought up by rail, could stop attackers in the open. Most attacks began with heavy bombardments, but these rarely destroyed the defences.

questions.stem: The first large-scale use of poison gas (chlorine) by the German army was at:
options: the Battle of the Somme in early July 1916
the Gallipoli landings in April 1915
the Battle of Verdun in February 1916
the Second Battle of Ypres in April 1915
questions.explanation: Chlorine was released against French colonial and Canadian troops near Ypres on 22 April 1915. Both sides then used gas, including phosgene and, from 1917, mustard gas, and gas masks became standard equipment.

questions.stem: Tanks were first used in battle by:
options: the Americans at Amiens in August 1918
the British on the Somme in September 1916
the French at Verdun in the spring of 1916
the Germans at Cambrai in November 1917
questions.explanation: British tanks went into action at Flers-Courcelette on 15 September 1916. Early tanks were slow and broke down often, but massed tanks were used more effectively at Cambrai in 1917 and Amiens in 1918.

questions.stem: How did the role of aircraft change during the war?
options: From dropping propaganda leaflets to replacing artillery as the main weapon
From reconnaissance and spotting for artillery to fighting for control of the air
From bombing enemy cities to carrying wounded soldiers back to base hospitals
From carrying troops behind enemy lines to sinking enemy submarines at sea
questions.explanation: Aircraft first served as the eyes of the army, photographing trenches and directing artillery fire. Fighters armed with machine guns firing through the propeller arc soon fought to protect or destroy these aircraft, and bombing developed later in the war.

questions.stem: Why did commanders on the Western Front often lose control of an attack once the troops left their trenches?
options: Senior officers stayed in Britain and sent all of their orders by telegram
Soldiers were forbidden to report back until the attack was over
Shellfire cut telephone lines, so messages depended on runners and pigeons
Radios were banned in case the enemy listened to every message sent
questions.explanation: Field telephones worked well behind the lines, but cables laid forward were easily cut. Runners, carrier pigeons, flares and lamps were slow or unreliable, so generals often did not know what was happening. Portable radio was still in its infancy.

questions.stem: Which medical development improved the survival of wounded soldiers during the war?
options: Aircraft that flew the seriously wounded straight back to Britain
Blood transfusion with stored blood and splints such as the Thomas splint
Antibiotics such as penicillin issued to every front-line medical unit
A vaccine against influenza given to all troops in the summer of 1918
questions.explanation: Methods for storing blood allowed transfusions near the front, and the Thomas splint, which immobilised broken thigh bones, greatly reduced deaths from those wounds. A chain of casualty clearing stations and hospitals also improved care. Penicillin was not used until the Second World War.

questions.stem: The Allied campaign at Gallipoli in 1915 aimed to:
options: defend the Suez Canal by invading the Ottoman homeland from the south
seize the oilfields of Mesopotamia before Germany could take them
force the Dardanelles, knock out the Ottoman Empire and open a route to Russia
capture Jerusalem and drive Ottoman forces out of Palestine and Syria
questions.explanation: After a naval attempt to force the straits failed on 18 March 1915, troops landed to clear the peninsula's defences. Success would have threatened Constantinople and opened a sea route to Russia. Palestine and Mesopotamia were separate campaigns.

questions.stem: Which statement about the landing at Anzac Cove on 25 April 1915 is accurate?
options: The landing met no resistance until the troops were in sight of Constantinople
Australian and New Zealand troops landed at Cape Helles beside the British
The landing followed the capture of the Dardanelles forts by the Allied fleet
The troops came ashore north of the planned beach, among steep ridges and gullies
questions.explanation: The Anzacs landed near Ari Burnu, north of the intended area, and faced rugged terrain and determined Ottoman defenders, including Mustafa Kemal's division. British and French troops landed at Cape Helles. The naval attack had already failed.

questions.stem: Which feature most distinguished the conditions faced by troops at Gallipoli from those on the Western Front?
options: There was no trench warfare, because the ground was too rocky to dig
They held small beachheads under fire, supplied entirely from the sea
Gas and tanks were used there far more often than in France and Belgium
The front lines moved hundreds of kilometres in each year of fighting
questions.explanation: At Anzac the front line was often only metres from the enemy and the whole position lay within range of Ottoman guns. Water, food and ammunition all came by boat, and disease such as dysentery was widespread. Both fronts were dominated by trenches.

questions.stem: Which part of the Gallipoli campaign is usually judged the most successful for the Allies?
options: The evacuation of December 1915 and January 1916, with very few casualties
The August offensive, which captured the heights of Sari Bair for good
The naval attack of March 1915, which destroyed the Ottoman forts on the straits
The landing at Suvla Bay, which broke through to the Dardanelles
questions.explanation: The evacuation was carefully planned and deceived the Ottoman forces, with devices such as self-firing rifles. The August offensive, including Lone Pine and the Nek, failed to take the main heights, and the Suvla landing stalled.

questions.stem: How did fighting on the Eastern Front differ from fighting on the Western Front?
options: Only cavalry units took part, as the roads were too poor for infantry
Its great length allowed more movement and much larger advances
It was fought without trenches, machine guns or heavy artillery
It was fought mainly by the navies on the Baltic and Black Seas
questions.explanation: With a front stretching over a thousand kilometres, lines were thinner and breakthroughs more common, as at Tannenberg in 1914 and in the German advance of 1915. Trenches and machine guns were still used, but the war of movement never ended there.

questions.stem: Germany attacked the French fortress city of Verdun in February 1916. Falkenhayn later wrote that his aim was to:
options: break through to the Channel ports and cut Britain off from France
draw British troops away from the fighting at Gallipoli
capture Paris in a single offensive before the Americans arrived
wear down the French army in a battle France could not abandon
questions.explanation: Falkenhayn claimed after the war that he chose Verdun because France would defend it at any cost. The battle lasted most of 1916 and caused huge losses on both sides, and French soldiers were rotated through it so that most of the army served there.

questions.stem: On 1 July 1916, the first day of the Battle of the Somme, the British Army suffered about 57,000 casualties. Which was the main reason?
options: The week-long bombardment had failed to cut the wire or destroy deep German dugouts
The Germans had used poison gas for the first time on the British part of the line
British troops attacked at night and lost their way in the unfamiliar ground
The French army withdrew from the attack at the last minute and exposed the flank
questions.explanation: British planners expected the bombardment to destroy the defences, but many shells were duds or shrapnel that did not cut wire, and Germans sheltered in deep dugouts. Troops advancing in daylight were cut down by machine guns. French units on the right of the attack made good gains.

questions.stem: The Battle of Fromelles on 19-20 July 1916 is remembered in Australia because:
options: the 5th Division suffered more than 5,500 casualties in about 24 hours
Australians captured the town of Fromelles and held it for the rest of the war
it was the first battle in which Australian troops fought alongside tanks
Monash used tanks, aircraft and artillery to win it in just 93 minutes
questions.explanation: The attack, intended to stop German troops moving to the Somme, failed with 5,533 Australian casualties, the worst 24 hours in Australian military history. Monash's 93-minute victory was at Hamel in July 1918.

questions.stem: Soldiers' accounts of the Third Battle of Ypres (Passchendaele) in late 1917 most often stress:
options: heavy rain and shelling that turned the battlefield into deep mud
rapid advances across open country by cavalry and armoured cars
extreme heat, thirst and flies in a summer campaign on hill slopes
street fighting in the ruins of Ypres after the town fell to Germany
questions.explanation: Constant shelling destroyed the drainage of the low-lying Flanders fields, and unusually heavy rain made a swamp in which men, horses and guns sank. Ypres itself remained in Allied hands throughout the war.

questions.stem: The term 'shell shock' came to describe:
options: wounds caused by metal fragments from bursting shells
a fever spread by lice among soldiers in the trenches
psychological breakdown caused by the stress of combat
permanent deafness caused by the noise of heavy artillery fire
questions.explanation: Doctors at first thought the symptoms came from the physical effects of explosions, but realised they could occur in men never near a shell. Lice spread trench fever, a different condition.

questions.stem: In the First World War, 'total war' meant:
options: a war fought only until one side's army was entirely destroyed
the use of every available weapon, including nuclear weapons
mobilising a nation's whole economy and society for the war effort
a war in which every country in the world took part on one side or the other
questions.explanation: Governments took control of industry, labour, food and information, and civilians became targets of blockade and bombing. Many countries stayed neutral, and nuclear weapons did not exist until 1945.

questions.stem: Britain's Defence of the Realm Act of August 1914 gave the government power to:
options: conscript every man aged 18 to 41 into the army from the start of the war
give the vote to women over 30 in return for their work in industry
deport anyone of German descent who had been born in Britain
censor the press, take over factories and land, and control daily life
questions.explanation: DORA allowed censorship, the requisitioning of property and controls such as shorter pub hours. Conscription came only with the Military Service Act of 1916, and women over 30 gained the vote in 1918. Australia's equivalent was the War Precautions Act 1914.

questions.stem: How did the war change the working lives of many women in Britain?
options: Many took jobs in munitions, transport and offices left by men who enlisted
Women were conscripted into front-line infantry units from 1916 onwards
Women were banned from paid work so that returning soldiers had jobs
Most women left factories to work on farms after food rationing began
questions.explanation: Women filled shells in munitions factories, drove trams and worked as clerks, and others served as nurses or in auxiliary services. Women did not serve as front-line infantry. Many lost these jobs when men returned after 1918.

questions.stem: In 1918 Britain gave the vote to women over 30 who met a property qualification. Which evaluation of the war's impact on British women is best supported?
options: War work strengthened the case for the vote, but many women lost their jobs when men returned
The war gave women equality with men in pay and the vote at 21 by the end of 1918
Women played no real part in war work, so the vote came only from prewar campaigning
Women's war work ended their interest in the vote, which they gained without asking
questions.explanation: Women's contribution made it hard to keep denying them the vote, although the prewar campaign also mattered and equal voting came only in 1928. After the war many women were pushed out of industry, so change was real but limited.

questions.stem: Australia's conscription referendums of 1916 and 1917:
options: were defeated in 1916 but passed in 1917 after the United States joined
were both defeated, and the first split the Labor Party under Hughes
were both passed, and conscripts were sent overseas from early 1918
were passed in 1916 but defeated in 1917 after the losses at Fromelles
questions.explanation: Prime Minister Billy Hughes put the question to voters in October 1916 and December 1917, and both were narrowly rejected after bitter campaigns. Hughes and his supporters left the Labor Party in 1916 and formed a new government. Australia's overseas forces stayed entirely volunteer.

questions.stem: The USA declared war on Germany in April 1917 mainly because of:
options: a treaty that committed the USA to defend Britain and France
German attacks on American colonies in the Pacific Ocean
unrestricted submarine warfare and the Zimmermann Telegram
the German invasion of Belgium and the sinking of HMS Dreadnought
questions.explanation: Germany resumed unrestricted submarine warfare in February 1917, sinking American ships, and the intercepted Zimmermann Telegram proposed a German alliance with Mexico. The USA had no alliance with the Entente and joined as an 'associated power'.

questions.stem: Germany's Spring Offensive, launched in March 1918, failed mainly because:
options: Russia rejoined the war and forced Germany to move its armies back east
American troops had already reached the Rhine before the attack began
the Kaiser abdicated in March and the new government called off the attack
its gains outran supplies, losses were heavy and no vital target was taken
questions.explanation: Freed by Russia's exit from the war, Germany used new infiltration tactics to make the biggest advances since 1914. But its best troops were lost, the advance outran its supplies, and Amiens and the Channel ports held. American troops were arriving in growing numbers.

questions.stem: Ludendorff called 8 August 1918, the first day of the Battle of Amiens, the 'black day' of the German army because:
options: the Allies used poison gas against German troops for the first time
German forces lost the last of their colonies in Africa that day
a mutiny in the German navy forced the Kaiser to leave the country
Allied forces broke through and many German soldiers surrendered
questions.explanation: British, Australian, Canadian and French forces using tanks, aircraft and artillery together advanced several kilometres, and large numbers of Germans surrendered. It began the Hundred Days offensive that ended with the armistice of 11 November 1918.

questions.stem: Which combination of factors best explains the Allied victory in 1918?
options: The success of the Gallipoli campaign and the fall of Constantinople in 1916
Germany's lack of artillery and the refusal of its allies to send any troops
The blockade, fresh American troops, and better combined-arms tactics in the Hundred Days
The capture of Berlin by Russian forces and the surrender of the German navy
questions.explanation: The blockade caused severe shortages in Germany, American manpower tipped the balance, and the Allies learned to coordinate infantry, tanks, aircraft and artillery. Germany's allies also collapsed in late 1918. Russia had left the war in March 1918 and Gallipoli failed.

questions.stem: Which four empires had collapsed by the end of the war or soon after?
options: German, Austro-Hungarian, Russian and Ottoman
British, French, Russian and Ottoman
German, Italian, Japanese and Austro-Hungarian
Russian, Ottoman, Chinese and Portuguese
questions.explanation: Revolution ended the Russian Empire in 1917, the Kaiser and the Habsburg emperor fell in November 1918, and the Ottoman Empire was broken up, ending in 1922. New states included Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia and the Baltic states.

questions.stem: The influenza pandemic of 1918-1919 reached Australia later than many countries mainly because:
options: maritime quarantine delayed its arrival until early 1919
Australian troops were kept in Europe until the pandemic ended
the government had vaccinated the whole population in 1918
the disease could not survive the long voyage across the tropics
questions.explanation: Quarantine at Australian ports delayed the more deadly wave until early 1919, but it still killed thousands of Australians. No influenza vaccine existed, and many troops returned in 1919.

questions.stem: In postwar Germany the 'stab-in-the-back' myth claimed that:
options: the Kaiser had started the war against the army's advice
the army had not been beaten in the field but betrayed at home
the Allies had broken the armistice terms by invading Germany
Austria-Hungary had secretly made peace and left Germany alone
questions.explanation: Because Germany surrendered while its armies were still on foreign soil, nationalists blamed socialists, Jews and the politicians who signed the armistice. The myth weakened the Weimar Republic and was exploited by the Nazis.
